profile.feeling: Summer, salads, tomato sauce – and the stock character of the unreliable friend (treulose Tomate).

examples.text: Für die Soße brauche ich ein Kilo Tomaten.
examples.tr: I need a kilo of tomatoes for the sauce.

examples.text: Die Tomaten im Garten sind endlich reif.
examples.tr: The tomatoes in the garden are finally ripe.

examples.text: Hast du Tomaten auf den Augen? Das Schild steht direkt vor dir!
examples.tr: Are you blind? (lit. Do you have tomatoes on your eyes?) The sign is right in front of you!

phrases.tr: to have tomatoes on one's eyes
phrases.meaning: to fail to notice something obvious
an unreliable friend who does not turn up or keep in touch (said jokingly)

synonyms.nuance: the usual word in Austria (der Paradeiser, plural Paradeiser)

etymology.text: Borrowed from French tomate or Spanish tomate, from Classical Nahuatl tomatl (“tomatillo”), the tomato proper being xītomatl.

funFacts: The Austrian Paradeiser comes from Paradiesapfel, “apple of paradise”.
pitfalls: Plural with -n: eine Tomate, zwei Tomaten.
das Tomatenmark is tomato paste – Mark here means “pulp”, not the currency.
subtleties: Botanically a fruit (a berry), but in German cooking it counts as Gemüse (more precisely Fruchtgemüse, “fruit vegetable”).

profile.feeling: Kitchen tears; cosy cooking smells.

examples.text: Beim Zwiebelschneiden muss ich immer weinen.
examples.tr: I always cry when I cut onions.

examples.text: Brate die Zwiebeln goldbraun an.
examples.tr: Fry the onions until golden brown.

examples.text: Im Herbst pflanzt man Tulpenzwiebeln.
examples.tr: Tulip bulbs are planted in autumn.

examples.text: Opa zog seine alte Zwiebel aus der Westentasche.
examples.tr: Grandpa pulled his old pocket watch out of his waistcoat pocket.

phrases.tr: to dress following the onion principle

synonyms.nuance: Berlin and northern colloquial word for onion

etymology.text: From Middle High German zwibel, zwibolle, from Old High German zwibollo, from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

funFacts: The onion-shaped domes of Bavarian and Austrian churches are called Zwiebeltürme (“onion towers”).
pitfalls: die Zwiebel is feminine; plural die Zwiebeln.
Frühlingszwiebel = spring onion (scallion), not a small onion.
subtleties: Zwiebel also means any plant bulb: Blumenzwiebel, Tulpenzwiebel.

profile.feeling: The heart of traditional German cooking: boiled, fried, mashed, in salads and dumplings.

senses.def: (slang) a German, “spud” – used mockingly, e.g. by young people from immigrant families

examples.text: Schälst du bitte die Kartoffeln?
examples.tr: Could you peel the potatoes, please?

examples.text: Zum Fisch gibt es Kartoffeln und Salat.
examples.tr: The fish comes with potatoes and salad.

examples.text: Die Kartoffeln lagern wir im Keller.
examples.tr: We store the potatoes in the cellar.

phrases.text: Die dümmsten Bauern haben die dicksten Kartoffeln.
phrases.tr: The stupidest farmers have the fattest potatoes.
phrases.meaning: luck often goes to those who do not deserve it

phrases.text: jemanden fallen lassen wie eine heiße Kartoffel
phrases.tr: to drop someone like a hot potato

phrases.text: Rein in die Kartoffeln, raus aus den Kartoffeln.
phrases.tr: Into the potatoes, out of the potatoes.
phrases.meaning: contradictory instructions given one after the other

synonyms.nuance: Austria and parts of southern Germany (der Erdapfel, plural Erdäpfel)
south-western dialects (e.g. Palatinate, Saarland)

etymology.text: From older Tartuffel or Tartüffel (18th c.), from Italian tartufolo, diminutive of tartufo (“truffle”), from Medieval Latin *territūberum or Latin terrae tūber (“tuber of the earth”). The use as an ethnic nickname is due to the prominence of potatoes in German cuisine.

funFacts: In 1756 Frederick the Great of Prussia ordered the cultivation of potatoes in the so-called Kartoffelbefehl (“potato order”).
The word comes from Italian tartufolo, “little truffle”.
pitfalls: Plural Kartoffeln; potato crisps are Chips and French fries are Pommes (frites) – not *Kartoffeln.
subtleties: In slang, Kartoffel can be a mocking name for a German; it is usually teasing, but it can hurt.

profile.feeling: Strong smell, Mediterranean cooking, vampire jokes.

examples.text: Hack den Knoblauch ganz fein.
examples.tr: Chop the garlic very finely.

examples.text: Wer viel Knoblauch isst, riecht am nächsten Tag noch danach.
examples.tr: Anyone who eats a lot of garlic still smells of it the next day.

examples.text: Im Volksglauben schützt Knoblauch vor Vampiren.
examples.tr: In folk belief, garlic protects against vampires.

synonyms.nuance: short, friendly everyday form
colloquial word in Austria and southern Germany

etymology.text: From Early New High German Knobloch, from Middle High German knobelouch, with dissimilation from klobelouch, from Old High German chlobalouh (literally “clove-leek”), from Proto-West Germanic *klobulauk; from now dialectal klieben (“to cleave”) and Lauch (“leek”).

funFacts: The old form was Klobelauch; the kl- changed to kn- in line with words for knobbly things such as Knopf, Knoten, Knolle.
pitfalls: No plural: to count, use eine Knoblauchzehe (a clove) or eine Knoblauchknolle (a bulb).
Masculine: der Knoblauch, like der Lauch.
subtleties: The second half of Knoblauch is Lauch (leek) – garlic is literally the “cleft leek”.

profile.feeling: Fresh salads in summer; in slang, mocking.

senses.def: piece of junk – an old, poor car or device

examples.text: Ich schneide eine Gurke für den Salat.
examples.tr: I'm slicing a cucumber for the salad.

examples.text: Die Gurken aus dem Garten sind dieses Jahr klein.
examples.tr: The cucumbers from the garden are small this year.

examples.text: Zum Abendbrot gibt es saure Gurken.
examples.tr: There are pickled gherkins with supper.

examples.text: Mit der alten Gurke fährst du noch?
examples.tr: You're still driving that old banger?

phrases.meaning: the silly season: summer, when there is little news

synonyms.nuance: the long fresh cucumber, as opposed to pickles
a small pickled gherkin

etymology.text: Borrowed from Old Polish ogórek, from Byzantine Greek ἀγγούριον (angoúrion, “cucumber”). Cognate with Dutch augurk, English gherkin.

funFacts: Gurke reached German through Polish from Byzantine Greek ἀγγούριον – the same word as Modern Greek αγγούρι.
pitfalls: German Gurke covers both the fresh cucumber and the small pickle; English separates cucumber and gherkin.
subtleties: In colloquial speech a Gurke is a lame old car or a useless device – context tells you which “cucumber” is meant.

profile.feeling: Mediterranean and Middle Eastern dishes; glossy purple.

senses.def: aubergine, eggplant (the plant and its fruit)

examples.text: Ich schneide die Aubergine in Scheiben und grille sie.
examples.tr: I slice the aubergine and grill it.

examples.text: Auberginen gibt es heute das ganze Jahr im Supermarkt.
examples.tr: Today aubergines are available in the supermarket all year round.

examples.text: In Wien sagt man Melanzani statt Aubergine.
examples.tr: In Vienna people say Melanzani instead of Aubergine.

synonyms.nuance: the Austrian word (die Melanzani, plural Melanzani)

etymology.text: Unadapted borrowing from French aubergine. Doublet of Melanzani.

funFacts: Aubergine and Austrian Melanzani are doublets – two borrowings that go back to the same source.
pitfalls: French spelling and pronunciation: Au- is said [o] and -g- like the s in “pleasure”: [obɛʁˈʒiːnə].
subtleties: aubergine is also a colour word: ein auberginefarbenes Kleid (an aubergine-coloured dress).

profile.feeling: Homely and healthy; children's food and rabbit jokes.

examples.text: Ich schäle die Karotten für die Suppe.
examples.tr: I'm peeling the carrots for the soup.

examples.text: Ein Kilo Karotten, bitte.
examples.tr: A kilo of carrots, please.

examples.text: Karotten sind gut für die Augen, sagt meine Oma.
examples.tr: Carrots are good for your eyes, my grandma says.

synonyms.nuance: the same vegetable; the usual word in northern and central Germany
southern Germany (Bavaria, Swabia)
Switzerland

etymology.text: Borrowed from French carotte, from Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτόν (kărōtón).

funFacts: The orange carrot is usually credited to Dutch growers of the 17th century; older carrots were mostly purple or yellow.
pitfalls: Spelling: German Karotte has one r and two t's; English carrot has two r's and one t.
subtleties: “Carrot and stick” is not said with Karotte in German: Zuckerbrot und Peitsche (“sweet bread and whip”).
Which word people use (Karotte, Möhre, Gelbe Rübe, Rüebli) tells you where they are from.

profile.feeling: Trendy, colourful, healthy – a newcomer to German kitchens.

senses.def: sweet potato (the plant and its tuber)

examples.text: Süßkartoffeln schmecken auch als Pommes sehr gut.
examples.tr: Sweet potatoes also taste great as fries.

examples.text: Ich backe die Süßkartoffel im Ofen.
examples.tr: I'm baking the sweet potato in the oven.

examples.text: Die Süßkartoffel ist mit der Kartoffel nicht näher verwandt.
examples.tr: The sweet potato is not closely related to the potato.

synonyms.nuance: the older, less common name (from Spanish batata), found in botany and some recipes

etymology.text: süß (“sweet”) + Kartoffel (“potato”).

funFacts: English potato itself comes from batata, the Caribbean word for the sweet potato.
pitfalls: In Switzerland ß is written ss: Süsskartoffel.
Plural Süßkartoffeln.
subtleties: Despite the name, the sweet potato belongs to the bindweed family (Windengewächse), not to the nightshade family like the potato.

profile.feeling: Small, green, a little childish: peas and carrots, pea soup.

senses.def: pea (the plant, the pod and the seed)

examples.text: Zum Mittagessen gibt es Erbsen und Möhren.
examples.tr: For lunch there are peas and carrots.

examples.text: Die Erbsen aus der Dose sind schon gekocht.
examples.tr: The tinned peas are already cooked.

examples.text: Die Prinzessin spürte die Erbse durch zwanzig Matratzen hindurch.
examples.tr: The princess felt the pea through twenty mattresses.

phrases.meaning: an over-sensitive, fussy person (after Andersen's fairy tale)

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym: Zuckererbse (sugar pea) and Kichererbse (chickpea) are different plants or kinds.

etymology.text: From Middle High German erbīz, erwīz, arwīz, ar(e)weiz, from Old High German arawīz, araweiz, from Proto-West Germanic *arwīt, *arwait. Cognate with Dutch erwt, Swedish ärta.

funFacts: Gregor Mendel discovered the laws of inheritance in the 19th century by crossing pea plants.
pitfalls: die Kichererbse is the chickpea – a different plant, despite the name.
Plural Erbsen.
subtleties: der Erbsenzähler (“pea counter”) is a pedant, a nitpicker – pejorative.

profile.feeling: Childhood memories – loved or hated – and the classic Spinat mit Spiegelei.

senses.def: spinach (the plant and its leaves as food)

examples.text: Spinat mit Spiegelei und Kartoffeln ist ein Klassiker.
examples.tr: Spinach with fried egg and potatoes is a classic.

examples.text: Den frischen Spinat musst du gründlich waschen.
examples.tr: You have to wash the fresh spinach thoroughly.

examples.text: Als Kind mochte ich keinen Spinat.
examples.tr: As a child I didn't like spinach.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; Blattspinat (leaf spinach) and Rahmspinat (creamed spinach) are forms in which it is sold.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Italian spinace.

funFacts: Italian spinace, like English spinach, goes back to Arabic إِسْفَانَاخ (ʔisfānāḵ), from Classical Persian.
pitfalls: Masculine: der Spinat. It is normally uncountable; the plural Spinate is only used for kinds of spinach.
subtleties: In shops you choose between Blattspinat (whole leaves) and Rahmspinat (chopped, with cream) – often frozen.

profile.feeling: Crunchy, peppery, red-and-white; bread-and-butter suppers.

examples.text: Ein Bund Radieschen kostet einen Euro.
examples.tr: A bunch of radishes costs one euro.

examples.text: Die Radieschen sind scharf und knackig.
examples.tr: The radishes are hot and crunchy.

examples.text: Der alte Pirat sieht sich die Radieschen jetzt von unten an.
examples.tr: The old pirate is pushing up daisies now (lit. looking at the radishes from below).

phrases.text: sich die Radieschen von unten ansehen
phrases.tr: to look at the radishes from below
phrases.meaning: to be dead and buried (like English “to push up daisies”)

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; der Rettich is the large radish, a different form of the plant.

etymology.text: Diminutive of earlier Radies, borrowed from Dutch radijs, itself from Middle French radice, from Italian radice, from Latin rādīx.

funFacts: Radieschen goes back to Latin rādīx “root” – the same word as English radish and radical.
pitfalls: das Radieschen (small red radish) is not der Rettich (large, usually white radish).
Plural unchanged: ein Radieschen, zwei Radieschen.
subtleties: Words in -chen are always neuter and do not change in the plural: das Radieschen, die Radieschen.

profile.feeling: Autumn: soups, Halloween lanterns, orange piles at farm stands.

senses.def: pumpkin, squash, gourd (any plant of the genus Cucurbita or its fruit)

examples.text: Zu Halloween schnitzen die Kinder Gesichter in Kürbisse.
examples.tr: At Halloween the children carve faces into pumpkins.

examples.text: Den Hokkaido-Kürbis muss man nicht schälen.
examples.tr: You don't need to peel the Hokkaido squash.

examples.text: Auf dem Markt liegen riesige Kürbisse.
examples.tr: There are huge pumpkins at the market.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in standard German; kinds are named by compounds (Hokkaido-Kürbis, Butternusskürbis, Riesenkürbis).

etymology.text: From Middle High German kürbiȥ, from Old High German kurbiȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *kurbit (ultimately from Latin cucurbita). Cognate with Luxembourgish Kürbis, Yiddish קירבעס (kirbes).

funFacts: The Austrian region of Styria (Steiermark) is famous for its dark green Kürbiskernöl, pumpkin-seed oil.
pitfalls: -is → -isse: der Kürbis, des Kürbisses, die Kürbisse, den Kürbissen.
subtleties: Kürbis covers what English splits into pumpkin, squash and gourd; kinds are named with compounds: Hokkaido-Kürbis, Butternusskürbis.

profile.feeling: Heat and fire – cooking with a kick.

examples.text: Vorsicht, die Chilis sind sehr scharf!
examples.tr: Careful, the chilies are very hot!

examples.text: Ich schneide einen Chili klein und gebe ihn in die Soße.
examples.tr: I chop a chili finely and add it to the sauce.

examples.text: Heute Abend gibt es Chili con Carne.
examples.tr: Tonight we're having chili con carne.

synonyms.nuance: the chili pod – unambiguous, never the powder or the dish
in Germany a (often pickled) hot pepper; in Switzerland Peperoni means the bell pepper
the Austrian word for a hot pepper

etymology.text: From Spanish chile, from Classical Nahuatl chīlli (etymology of the English cognate chili).

funFacts: The heat of chilies comes from capsaicin (Capsaicin); birds do not feel it, mammals do.
pitfalls: Gender varies: der Chili is the usual dictionary form, but die Chili is also heard, and Wiktionary lists masculine, feminine and neuter.
Peperoni is a pepper in German, not the sausage – that is a salami.
subtleties: Chili can mean the fresh pod, the powder or the dish; context decides.

profile.feeling: Hearty winter food – cabbage rolls, sauerkraut, red cabbage with roast.

senses.def: cabbage (plants of the genus Brassica, especially the head cabbage)

examples.text: Im Winter essen wir oft Kohl mit Kartoffeln.
examples.tr: In winter we often eat cabbage with potatoes.

examples.text: Aus Weißkohl macht man Sauerkraut.
examples.tr: Sauerkraut is made from white cabbage.

examples.text: Red keinen Kohl!
examples.tr: Don't talk rubbish!

phrases.text: Das macht den Kohl auch nicht fett.
phrases.tr: That doesn't make the cabbage fat either.
phrases.meaning: that doesn't help much / makes no real difference
an old story or idea served up again

synonyms.nuance: cabbage in Austria and southern Germany (Weißkraut, Blaukraut)
western and central German word for cabbage; also “nonsense”
specifically the white head cabbage

etymology.text: From Middle High German kōl, from Old High German kōl, kōlo, kōli, ultimately from Latin caulis.

funFacts: The surname Kohl originally named a grower or seller of cabbages.
pitfalls: der Kohl (cabbage) ≠ die Kohle (coal; colloquially also “money”) – and the rare plural of Kohl is also Kohle.
Usually uncountable: Kohl essen; for one head say ein Kohlkopf.
subtleties: The kinds are compounds: Rotkohl (in the south Blaukraut or Rotkraut), Weißkohl, Grünkohl, Rosenkohl, Blumenkohl.

profile.feeling: Mild and creamy-white; Sunday lunch with cheese sauce.

examples.text: Der Blumenkohl wird mit Käse überbacken.
examples.tr: The cauliflower is baked with a cheese topping.

examples.text: Ein Kopf Blumenkohl reicht für vier Personen.
examples.tr: One head of cauliflower is enough for four people.

examples.text: In Österreich heißt der Blumenkohl Karfiol.
examples.tr: In Austria cauliflower is called Karfiol.

synonyms.nuance: the Austrian word (der Karfiol), from Italian cavolfiore

etymology.text: Blume (“flower”) + -n- + Kohl (“cabbage”).

funFacts: A boxer's swollen ear is a Blumenkohlohr, just like English “cauliflower ear”.
Both Blumenkohl and Austrian Karfiol (Italian cavolfiore) mean “flower cabbage”.
pitfalls: Masculine like Kohl: der Blumenkohl. Compounds take the gender of their last part.
subtleties: The florets are called Röschen, “little roses”.

profile.feeling: Healthy green trees on the plate – for some children a punishment.

examples.text: Brokkoli dämpfe ich nur ein paar Minuten.
examples.tr: I steam broccoli for just a few minutes.

examples.text: Die Kinder essen den Brokkoli heute ohne zu meckern.
examples.tr: Today the children are eating the broccoli without moaning.

examples.text: Brokkoli enthält viel Vitamin C.
examples.tr: Broccoli contains a lot of vitamin C.

synonyms.nuance: the Italian spelling – still correct and seen on menus and packaging, but less common

etymology.text: 18th century, from Italian broccoli. The usual pronunciation with a long /oː/ is perhaps influenced by the French spelling brocoli, formerly also found in German texts. The sense “marijuana” comes from a widely mocked remark by the federal drug commissioner Daniela Ludwig at a press conference in 2020.

funFacts: In 2020 the German drug commissioner said at a press conference that cannabis was „kein Brokkoli“ (no broccoli); the much-mocked remark made Brokkoli jokey slang for marijuana.
pitfalls: Plural unchanged: der Brokkoli, die Brokkoli.
Spelling with kk: Brokkoli (the Italian spelling Broccoli is also accepted).
subtleties: Most Germans say it with a long o, [ˈbroːkoli] – unlike Italian broccoli with a short o.

profile.feeling: Soups and quiches; in youth slang, a skinny weakling.

examples.text: Schneide den Lauch in feine Ringe.
examples.tr: Cut the leek into thin rings.

examples.text: Für die Suppe brauchen wir zwei Stangen Lauch.
examples.tr: We need two leeks (lit. stalks of leek) for the soup.

examples.text: Du Lauch, nicht mal eine Kiste kannst du tragen!
examples.tr: You weakling, you can't even carry a crate!

collocations.tr: a leek (lit. a stalk of leek)

synonyms.nuance: the same vegetable; more common in northern Germany

etymology.text: From Middle High German louch, from Old High German louh, from Proto-West Germanic *lauk, from Proto-Germanic *laukaz. Compare Low German Look, Dutch look, English leek, Danish løg, Swedish lök.

funFacts: Lauch hides in Knoblauch (garlic), Schnittlauch (chives) and Bärlauch (wild garlic).
pitfalls: Lauch alone is the leek; Schnittlauch is chives and Knoblauch is garlic.
subtleties: As slang (Du Lauch!) it is an insult for a skinny, weak person – common among young people.

profile.feeling: Bright red, yellow and green – crunchy in salads, stuffed with rice; also the spice.

examples.text: Ich schneide eine rote Paprika in Streifen.
examples.tr: I'm cutting a red pepper into strips.

examples.text: Gefüllte Paprika mit Reis mag ich sehr.
examples.tr: I really like stuffed peppers with rice.

examples.text: Das Gulasch braucht einen Löffel Paprika.
examples.tr: The goulash needs a spoonful of paprika.

synonyms.nuance: the vegetable, never the spice
in Switzerland the usual word for the bell pepper (in Germany Peperoni are hot peppers)

etymology.text: Borrowed from Hungarian paprika, from Serbo-Croatian pàprika, from pȁpar, from Proto-Slavic *pьpьrь, from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”), from Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippali, “long pepper”).

funFacts: The Hungarian scientist Albert Szent-Györgyi isolated vitamin C in quantity from paprika peppers and won the 1937 Nobel Prize.
pitfalls: Gender: Wiktionary gives both der and die Paprika. In Germany die Paprika is usual for the vegetable; der Paprika is the form used in Austria; for the spice both genders occur.
Plural: Paprika after an article or number (zwei Paprika), but often Paprikas when it stands alone (Ich kaufe Paprikas).
subtleties: Paprika is both the vegetable and the spice; Paprikaschote is unambiguous.

profile.feeling: Earthy, sweet and blood-red – it stains everything it touches.

examples.text: Die Rote Bete muss ungefähr eine Stunde kochen.
examples.tr: The beetroot has to boil for about an hour.

examples.text: Rote Bete färbt die Hände rot.
examples.tr: Beetroot stains your hands red.

examples.text: In der Schweiz sagt man Rande statt Rote Bete.
examples.tr: In Switzerland people say Rande instead of Rote Bete.

synonyms.nuance: the usual word in Austria and southern Germany
the Swiss word (die Rande, plural Randen)
a very common spelling variant of the same word

etymology.text: rot (“red”) + Bete (“beet”); Bete is borrowed from Middle Low German bête, from Old Saxon *bēta, from Proto-West Germanic *bētā (“beet”), ultimately from Latin bēta.

funFacts: The red colour (betanin) is used as a natural food colouring, E 162 (beetroot red).
pitfalls: Rote is an adjective and is declined: die Rote Bete, der Roten Bete, mit Roter Bete (without article), die Roten Beten, but Rote Beten (plural without article).
Do not confuse Bete/Beete with das Beet (flower bed).
subtleties: It is often used as an uncountable noun even for several roots: Ich esse gern Rote Bete.

profile.feeling: Summer gardens that produce far too much.

examples.text: Die Zucchini schneide ich in dünne Scheiben.
examples.tr: I cut the courgette into thin slices.

examples.text: Im August wachsen im Garten mehr Zucchini, als wir essen können.
examples.tr: In August more courgettes grow in the garden than we can eat.

examples.text: Gegrillte Zucchini passen gut zum Fleisch.
examples.tr: Grilled courgettes go well with meat.

synonyms.nuance: the Swiss word (die Zucchetti)

etymology.text: Borrowed from Italian zucchini, plural of zucchino.

funFacts: zucchini means “little pumpkins”: Italian zucca = pumpkin, gourd.
pitfalls: Singular and plural are the same: die Zucchini – die Zucchini (colloquially also Zucchinis).
subtleties: German uses the Italian plural zucchini as its singular; the “correct” Italian singular der Zucchino is rare.

profile.feeling: Hearty: green beans with bacon, bean stews, coffee beans.

senses.def: bean; as a vegetable especially the green bean (grüne Bohne)

examples.text: Zum Braten gibt es grüne Bohnen.
examples.tr: There are green beans with the roast.

examples.text: Bohnen muss man gut durchkochen, roh sind sie giftig.
examples.tr: Beans must be cooked through; raw they are poisonous.

examples.text: Ich mahle die Bohnen für den Kaffee frisch.
examples.tr: I grind the beans for the coffee fresh.

phrases.meaning: not at all, not in the least

phrases.tr: to have beans in one's ears
phrases.meaning: not to listen, to ignore what is said

synonyms.nuance: unambiguous name of the fresh green pod
the Austrian word for the green bean
pole bean, a climbing kind of green bean
bush bean, a low-growing kind of green bean

etymology.text: From Middle High German bone, from Old High German bōna, from Proto-West Germanic *baunu, from Proto-Germanic *baunō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”). Compare Dutch boon, English bean, Danish bønne.

funFacts: Bohnenkraut (savory) is a herb, not a bean – it got its name because it is cooked with beans.
pitfalls: Bohne alone can be a green bean, a dried bean or a coffee bean – say grüne Bohnen for the vegetable.
subtleties: eine Bohnenstange (“beanpole”) is a very tall, thin person.

profile.feeling: Fresh green rings on salads and Asian dishes.

examples.text: Ich schneide die Frühlingszwiebeln in feine Ringe.
examples.tr: I cut the spring onions into thin rings.

examples.text: Ein Bund Frühlingszwiebeln, bitte.
examples.tr: A bunch of spring onions, please.

examples.text: Frühlingszwiebeln schmecken gut im Rührei.
examples.tr: Spring onions taste good in scrambled eggs.

collocations.tr: to cut spring onions into rings
the green part of the spring onions

synonyms.nuance: the same vegetable; a very common name in shops

etymology.text: Frühling (“spring”) + Zwiebel (“onion”).

funFacts: The compound takes the gender of its last part: die Zwiebel → die Frühlingszwiebel.
pitfalls: Note the linking -s-: Frühling-s-zwiebel.
It is not a small onion (Perlzwiebel) or a shallot (Schalotte).
subtleties: Both the white bulb and the green leaves are eaten.

profile.feeling: Crunchy green stalks: soups, sauces and healthy snacks.

examples.text: Staudensellerie mit Dip ist ein gesunder Snack.
examples.tr: Celery with a dip is a healthy snack.

examples.text: Für die Bolognese brauche ich Karotten, Zwiebeln und Staudensellerie.
examples.tr: For the Bolognese I need carrots, onions and celery.

examples.text: Den Staudensellerie gibt es im Supermarkt das ganze Jahr.
examples.tr: Celery is available in the supermarket all year round.

synonyms.nuance: the same vegetable, another common name
the general word – but in Germany plain Sellerie often means the celeriac root (Knollensellerie)

etymology.text: Staude (“perennial plant, shrub”) + -n- + Sellerie; Sellerie is borrowed from French céleri, from Lombard selleri, from Latin selīnum, from Ancient Greek σέλῑνον (sélīnon).

funFacts: Sellerie goes back to Ancient Greek σέλινον – Modern Greek still calls celery σέλινο.
pitfalls: In Germany plain Sellerie usually means the round celeriac root; for the stalks say Staudensellerie or Stangensellerie.
Gender varies: der or die Staudensellerie (Wiktionary lists both).
subtleties: Staude refers to the bushy, perennial plant – the stalks grow as a dense bunch.

profile.feeling: Summer fields of tall plants; corn on the cob at barbecues; popcorn.

senses.def: maize, corn (the plant and its grains; also sweet corn as a vegetable)

examples.text: Auf dem Feld wächst Mais.
examples.tr: Maize is growing in the field.

examples.text: Ich gebe eine Dose Mais in den Salat.
examples.tr: I'm putting a tin of sweetcorn into the salad.

examples.text: Den Mais grillen wir direkt am Kolben.
examples.tr: We grill the corn right on the cob.

synonyms.nuance: Austrian and Bavarian word for maize
specifically sweet corn, the vegetable

etymology.text: From Spanish maíz, from Taíno *mahis, *mahisi.

funFacts: des Mais can also be the genitive of der Mai (May) – the two words only look alike.
pitfalls: False friend: German Korn is grain (or a grain spirit), not corn; corn is Mais.
Usually no plural: for one cob say ein Maiskolben.
subtleties: Mais is both the farm crop (Futtermais, animal feed) and the vegetable (Zuckermais).
